1:
Ellicott begins with the word: sign is better than wonder, for this is not a mere wonder but something which has a meaning — not a surprise ending with itself, but a signal to arrest attention, with an idea concealed behind it. Robertson notes she is the earliest female figure in the Apocalyptic vision. That she is the Church nearly all grant; where they part is on which Church, and when.

The two oldest voices read the emblems as a single picture. Victorinus takes her for the ancient Church of fathers, prophets and apostles, which had the groans of its longing until it saw Christ, the fruit of its people according to the flesh. Clothed with the sun intimates the hope of resurrection and the glory of the promise; the moon intimates the fall of the bodies of the saints under the obligation of death — and the hope of those that sleep is not extinguished absolutely, but they have in their darkness a light such as the moon. The crown is the choir of fathers of whom Christ was to take flesh. Bede reads the same moon through a psalm: peace will increase until it consume all the changeableness of mortality, and then death, the last enemy, will be destroyed. His woman is clothed with the light of Christ and treads upon temporal glory; the sign is one which appears in the Church still, that God is born of man.

The later readings turn the emblems into doctrine. Henry has her clothed with the sun as the imputed righteousness of Christ, so that she shines in his rays; the moon under her feet is the world, on which she stands but above which she lives; the crown of twelve stars is the gospel preached by the twelve apostles. Ellicott hears the Canticles behind the description — who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun — and makes the moon a token that she rises superior to all change. Wesley alone assigns the lights politically: the sun may betoken the Christian world, the moon the Mahometans, who also carry the moon in their ensigns, and the twelve stars the tribes of Israel, which are smaller than the sun and moon.

On the date they scatter. Gill sets the vision in the apostles’ times and the purer ages, under the Heathen and Arian persecutions, and reads her pregnancy as the kingdom of Christ about to be set up in the Roman empire. Clarke dates the travail to the persecutions, above all the long and most dreadful one under Diocletian; he also collects the rabbinical phrasing behind the chapter, in which the injured woman with child of the law of the striving men is the Israelitish Church. Barnes states the alternative most sharply: if the woman is the Church before the Saviour’s birth, the man child is Christ himself — but there is a harshness in representing the Saviour as the Son of the church, and such imagery is not found elsewhere in the Bible, where Christ is rather the Husband of the church than the Son. Robertson rules out one candidate: she is certainly not the Virgin Mary, as the last verse makes clear.

On her crying out, Robertson notes a word for torment used nowhere else in the New Testament of childbirth. Ellicott makes the pain structural: it is the law of her life that she must bring forth Christ to the world, and not simply that she must encounter pain, but that she cannot work deliverance without knowing suffering. Bede had already put the same thing as a paradox — the Church both brings forth those with whom it travails and ceases not to travail with them when already born. Wesley reads the cries as the painful longings, sighs and prayers of the saints for the coming of the kingdom.
3:
What is a dragon? Barnes goes to the naturalists and finds a creature largely assembled by imagination: vast in size, with something like a beard or dew-lap, three rows of teeth, and a breath that drew in not only the air but the birds flying over it; Robertson traces it through the poets and neighbouring nations — the Babylonians feared a seven-headed hydra, Typhon was the Egyptian dragon who persecuted Osiris — and allows himself one speculation nobody else here would make: one wonders whether these and the Chinese dragons are not race memories of conflicts with the diplodocus and like monsters.

Clarke asks why a dragon rather than any other fabulous beast, and answers from military history. In Daniel the kingdom of the Greeks is a he-goat for no apparent reason but that the goat was its national military standard; so the pagan Roman empire is called a dragon on a similar account, and it is very remarkable that the dragon was the principal Roman standard next to the eagle from the second century to the fifth. He produces the evidence: a handbook says the first standard of the whole legion is the eagle, which the aquilifer carries, while dragons are borne to battle by the draconarii — ten draconarii to one aquilifer, since a legion had ten cohorts. On his reading the beast is the heathen Roman empire, and a fabulous animal is a most proper emblem of a religion built mostly upon fable.

Ellicott takes the heads and horns as a statement about the shape of evil. The dragon is one, yet diverse: one as an evil spirit, diverse in the varieties of his power. The woman is but one; her foe is multiform. She has one work to do, and can but fulfil it in her Master’s way, whereas evil is bound by no law, regards no scruple, and works through any channel. He hears in the sevenfold kingship an assumption of divine similitude, a kingdom which is in much a parody of the true one. Robertson keeps the crowns precise: these are diadems, the band with which Persian kings bound on the tiara, not a victor’s wreath — and if Christ has many diadems, it is not strange that Satan should wear seven. Wesley adds that they are not properly crowns but costly bindings, for though fallen he was a great potentate still.

On the tail Gill supplies natural history: there are dragons whose power is not in their teeth but their tails, doing more hurt by striking than biting, and he recalls the serpent an ancient general fought, which dashed soldiers to pieces. Barnes reasons from the fraction: a power sweeping away all the stars would be universal, so one-third represents a dominion of that extent only — and he finds the fit in a period when the empire stood tripartite, part tolerating the church while the rest warred on it. Ellicott reads the stars as persons: light-bearers given high place that they might be burning and shining lights, dragged down to the low level of a life enslaved to evil.

On the dragon waiting to devour, two independently reach for the same two tyrants. Ellicott says our minds go back to Pharaoh, setting a watch for the offspring of Israel, and even more to Herod seeking the life of the infant Christ, on which last the vision seems primarily built — though its meaning is wider, since the same hostility is active against his children. Robertson arrives by grammar at the same pair: the verb is a graphic imperfect, the challenge of a dragon to a woman about to give birth — this is what Pharaoh did to Israel, and precisely so the devil tried to destroy the child Jesus. Wesley alone dates the sweeping of the stars between 847 and 947, when pestilent doctrines drew abundance of people from the truth.
5:
Who is the man child? The chapter divides five ways. Ellicott says there can be no doubt it is Christ, the combination of features being too distinct — the one who will feed his flock like a shepherd, who is to have all nations as his inheritance, and whose rule is supreme and irresistible. Robertson agrees: a direct reference to the birth of Jesus from Mary, who represented in her person the ideal woman. Wesley narrows it: Christ, considered not in his person but in his kingdom. Gill denies the personal reading: not Christ literally, but Christ mystically, in his members, or rather a more glorious breaking forth of his kingdom in the empire. Clarke is the most specific: the man child is the dynasty of Christian emperors, beginning with Constantine’s public acknowledgment of his belief late in 312, after the defeat of Maxentius; and the throne of God to which the child is caught up is the Roman throne, so called because there is no power but of God.

On the rod of iron the readings are gentler than the phrase. Barnes takes the verb from the psalm as a shepherd’s word, so the rule is irresistible as an iron sceptre is unbreakable, yet of a character of protection rather than force, like a shepherd’s sway over his flock. Cyril of Jerusalem, on the same psalm, takes the rod of iron for the kingdom of the Romans, and joins to it the stone cut out of a mountain without hands, not set up by human contrivance, which should overpower the whole world.

Ellicott will not let the identification narrow the vision: that the child is Christ must not limit the meaning to the evil one’s efforts against the infant Jesus, for it is also the Christ in the Church which the wicked one hates, and wherever Christ dwells in any heart by faith the foe will be found, ready to carry away the good seed. Robertson notes what the vision omits: the ministry, crucifixion and resurrection are passed over, the point being only that the dragon’s vigilance was futile.

Two make the flight begin at her worldly triumph, by different routes. Gill dates the disappearance of the true church to just after her advance, for through the riches and honours Constantine bestowed the Christians became vain, proud and careless, false doctrine obtained, and the antichristian apostasy came on. Clarke puts the flight immediately after the child is caught up, to denote the rapid increase of heresies after Christianity was made the religion of the empire. Barnes reads the wilderness as a place of few or no inhabitants, where the church became obscure yet mysteriously nourished — the church during the corruptions of the Papacy and the darkness of the middle ages. Robertson hears the whole biblical family of flights: Israel’s wanderings, Elijah’s, the Jews’ from Antiochus, the flight into Egypt, that of Christians at the destruction of Jerusalem.

The twelve hundred and sixty days are counted three ways. Barnes takes them as prophetic days, a day for a year, so twelve hundred and sixty years. Ellicott makes the number the period of the Church’s witness against predominant evil, matching the forty-two months of the witnesses; driven forth, her voice, though but as one crying in the wilderness, is lifted up for righteousness. Wesley alone gives dates: following another writer he makes the figure not twelve hundred and sixty but seven hundred and seventy-seven common years, 847 to 1524, and locates the wilderness in the European countries on this side the Danube, chiefly Bohemia, since Asia and Africa were in the hands of the Turks and Saracens. Cyril of Jerusalem, on the flight itself, divides the church: let those of us who are fearful provide for our own safety, and those who are of a good courage stand fast, for I do not despair of the Church’s nerves.
7:
Who is Michael? Barnes reports that many Protestant interpreters have supposed Christ, and that the reasons alleged are many of them very fanciful; he takes the name from Daniel, where Michael is the guardian angel of the people of God, and argues that if Christ had been intended, it is inconceivable why he was not called by his own name. Ellicott finds the identification doubtful, since Daniel calls Michael one of the chief princes, which almost suggests conflict among the spiritual hierarchies; the name, which means who is like unto God, may be a general one for any who represent the cause of God. Wesley presses hardest: that Michael is a created angel appears from his not daring, in disputing with Satan, to bring a railing accusation, but only saying, The Lord rebuke thee — and this modesty is implied in his name, for the name of Michael asks, Who is like God? Not Satan; not the highest archangel. Henry makes the party Christ, the great Angel of the covenant, and his faithful followers; Clarke identifies Michael with the man child, the dynasty of Christian emperors.

Where is the war? Gill is the most careful to say what it is not: not the third heaven, the habitation of God, for there is no discord there, but the church below, or rather the Roman empire, the heaven of Satan — and it refers neither to the dispute over the body of Moses, nor the original fall of the angels, nor the standing enmity of the two seeds, nor the combats Christ himself had with Satan. Clarke makes heaven the throne of the Roman empire, so the war is civil commotion among its governors. Barnes declines the literal reading: a vision passed before John as if there were a conflict, though it is not to be understood as a real transaction. Henry puts it in the church, the kingdom of heaven on earth.

Robertson rejects one option, then reaches for a modern illustration. The reference is not to the original rebellion of Satan; rather, as the coming of Christ brought fresh manifestations of diabolic power, so his return to heaven is pictured as the occasion of renewed attacks there. We are not to visualise it too literally, he says — but certainly modern airplanes help us grasp the notion of battles in the sky even more than the phalanxes of storm-clouds.

Ellicott reads the placement of the passage as its interpretation. We shall fail to catch its meaning if we detach it from its context, and the structure of the chapter warns against doing so. The narrative of the woman’s flight is suspended that this passage may be inserted — could we have a clearer indication of the writer’s anxiety to connect the war with the birth and rapture of the man child? The child is born a conqueror, and his rapture is the announcement that there, in the very highest, he is acknowledged victor. There is mystery about the war, but none about the occasion: it is the victory of Bethlehem, Calvary and Olivet, whose effects transcend things seen.

On the defeat Ellicott finds a general law: their power failed them, for there is an inherent weakness in evil, a spot which may be touched whereupon all its vaunted strength withers; and so complete was the overthrow that even their place knew them no more — I went by, and, lo, he was gone. Robertson admits the difficulty: the dragon is finally expelled, though to us it seems a difficult conception that Satan ever had access to heaven. Wesley feels the same weight and leaves it — so till now he had a place in heaven; how deep a mystery is this! Clarke finds the fulfilment in history: the success of Constantine over all his enemies, and his final triumph over Licinius, correspond exactly to the symbolical language of the verse.
9:
The verse hands out four names at once, and the first question is whether they are literal. Clarke says they cannot be: if by the dragon we understand the great spiritual enemy of mankind, we are necessarily led to the conclusion that the apostate spirit is a monster with seven heads and ten horns, and a tail dragging the third part of the stars. The appellations must therefore be figurative, of the heathen power — that old serpent, from its subtlety against the Christians; the devil, from its false accusations against the true worshippers of God; and Satan, since the Hebrew word signifies an adversary, from its persecutions of the Church. Barnes and Robertson read the same names of a person. Barnes allows that the language alludes to something which actually occurred at some far-distant period, when Satan was ejected — our Saviour seems to refer to it in saying, I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven — while holding that the event here symbolises a later crisis.

They also date the casting down differently, and the tenses are worth setting side by side. Ellicott has it accomplished: the stronger than the strong one has come and taken away his armour, the death-blow is given, and the prince of this world is judged. Clarke has it accomplished slowly and in the public record: the work of no single reign, since paganism took several mortal strokes under Constantine and his sons, was further reduced by Jovian, Valentinian and Valens, and was finally suppressed by the edicts of Gratian and Theodosius; not till 388 was Rome itself generally reformed, and about 395 the dragon may be considered in an eminent sense cast into the earth. Robertson has it still ahead: this vision of final victory has not come yet, but it is coming, and the hope of it should be a spur to missionary activity and zeal.

Gill supplies the detail that most nearly touches Clarke’s reading, from the emperor himself. Constantine speaks of the dragon removed from the government of the commonwealth by the providence of God and by his own ministry; and he had his effigies set before his palace porch, the cross over his head and a dragon under his feet, thrust through with darts and falling headlong. Clarke adds a rabbinical parallel in which God casts out Samael and his troops from the place of their holiness.

On the names the notes are complementary. Wesley points out that the two chief names mean exactly the same thing, one Greek and one Hebrew, and that dragons are a kind of large serpent, the shape intimating a poisonous and cruel disposition. Ellicott takes the serpent as emblem of the evil principle, whose head is now bruised, and the devil as accuser and calumniator — the accuser of the brethren in the next verse. Robertson notes that the ancient serpent is so called from a word meaning beginning, just as Jesus said the devil was a murderer from the beginning; and on the deceiving he observes that this is not an incident but an occupation — Satan can almost lead astray the very elect, so artful is he in his beguilings as he teaches us how to deceive ourselves.

Two attend to what the verse does not quite say. Wesley notices that at the casting out it is not yet said unto the earth: he was cast out of heaven, and at this the inhabitants of heaven rejoice; and when the earth is named, he adds that the enemy had not been unemployed there before, although his ordinary abode was in heaven. Robertson makes the same point from the other side — the earth was no new sphere of Satan’s working — and observes that the one verb for casting down is used three times over, of the dragon, of him again, and of his angels: the expulsion is complete.
10:
Accuser of the brethren is a title with a history, which Clarke assembles: nothing is more common in the rabbinical writings than Satan as the accuser of the Israelites, and the Greek word used here appears there transliterated into Hebrew letters. He quotes two: that if a man lives a holy life, then Satan stands and accuses him; and that the devil stands always as accuser before the King of Israel. Ellicott adds the answering title — in Jewish writings Michael is the advocate, standing in opposition to the accuser — and reports the tradition that Satan accuses men every day but the Day of Atonement. Robertson complicates this from the papyri: the odd form of the word was once thought a transliteration of a Hebrew one, but it turns up in a fourth-century magical papyrus with no sign of Jewish or Christian influence.

Two read the tense of the accusation, and both make it habitual: Ellicott says read not who accused but who accuseth, night and day; Robertson calls it the devil’s constant occupation. Wesley draws a quieter inference: the accuser of our brethren, that is, so long as they remained on earth — therefore this great voice was the voice of men only. Barnes finds the tenderness in the same words: the song is sung in heaven, by those whose brethren were still suffering persecution on earth — it shows the interest that they who have passed the flood have in the trials of those below. Ellicott hears in the doxology an echo of the Lord’s Prayer — the petition Thy kingdom come seems answered — though what is described is not the full establishment of the kingdom but its manifestation.

On how they overcame, two agree on a preposition. Gill takes the loud voice as the empire itself rejoicing, heaven being the empire now Christian, and makes the plainest image of the blood: under this purple covering they went triumphantly to glory. It is not by the blood but on account of it: Robertson says the blood is presented as the ground of the victory and not the means, though both ideas are true. Ellicott presses the second ground the same way: their victory is in virtue of the word to which they bore witness, not because they had a word of God but because they bore witness to it. Barnes locates the verse in the martyr age: no design was ever more ineffectual than crushing the church by persecution, and it was then that the world was constrained to acknowledge that the persecuted religion had a heavenly origin.

Ellicott refuses to let the last clause belong to the martyrs alone: in the martyr we have the fullest token of that devotion which loves Christ more than life, but many lose their lives for Christ’s sake who are never called to lay them down. Wesley gives names and dates: a king of Sweden slain about 900 for refusing to worship an idol, and Bohemian Christians in 916 under a persecuting queen.

The woe is not a wish: Barnes calls it not an imprecation but a prediction, and says dwellers on land and sea alike have cause to mourn. Clarke maps them: the earth is the people subject to the Roman empire, the sea those dominions reduced to anarchy by barbarous incursions. Ellicott keeps the verb exact — those who tabernacle in the heavens, not dwell — and hears in the wrath the poets’ unconquerable will and courage never to submit or yield. Henry states the law in a line: the rage of Satan grows so much the greater as he is limited both in place and time. Robertson puts the balance shortly — heaven has cause to rejoice, and earth reason to mourn — while Wesley alone computes the short time, four-fifths of an age, somewhat above 888 years, running from 947 to 1836.
13:
What are the two wings? Gill lists four readings and rejects all: not the two testaments; not faith and hope, by which she rose and dwelt on high; not prayer and good works; and not two kingdoms within the dominions of the dragon, France and Spain, where Christians were sheltered under Diocletian — for that was before the war in heaven. Clarke and Wesley agree on a fifth: the great eagle is the Roman empire, the two wings its eastern and western divisions.

Clarke grounds that on the standard. The Roman power is called an eagle from its legionary standard, introduced only in the second year of the consulate of Marius; before that, minotaurs, wolves, leopards, horses, boars and eagles were used indifferently, at the commander’s humour. The eagles were figures in relief of silver or gold, borne on pikes, wings displayed, often a thunderbolt in their talons. He dates the division to the seventeenth of January, 395, and observes that the wings could be given her because Christianity was by then established in both empires. Wesley says it more warmly: both the emperors now lent their wings to the woman, and provided a safe abode for her. Robertson lowers the bird: this is the generic article, since every eagle had two wings, and the creature meant is probably the griffon or vulture.

Ellicott reads the verse as a lesson in how deliverance comes. The serpent drives her into the wilderness, yet there her place is prepared by God; the way that seems hard is the way that is most blest, and neither the eagle power nor the heavenly sustenance had been hers without the serpent’s hate. He sharpens it against the Exodus parallel: there God bore Israel on eagles’ wings, but here the wings are given to the woman — the strength of the earlier dispensation is one used for, rather than in, the people of God, whereas the strength of the latter is in them. The place is not a chance spot but one prepared: the wicked one can never drive us from God’s place, only to it, unless we are enemies to ourselves.

Barnes supplies the precedent for a desert refuge — David fleeing there from Saul, Elijah from Jezebel — and insists on the nourishing: not that the church would flourish, but that in a long obscurity it would be kept alive. On the season and seasons and half a season he takes the reckoning of the earlier verse: forty-two months, twelve hundred and sixty days, and, as prophetic days, twelve hundred and sixty years. Robertson notes what this verse adds — from the face of the serpent, because the serpent rules the earth for that period — and concludes that to the end of the present order the Church dwells in the wilderness, and yet we must carry on for Christ.

On whether the period can be dated at all the chapter divides sharply. Ellicott says it is not to be sought by any effort to find some historical period, the three years and a half being the period of the Church’s trouble. Clarke argues the history in the other direction, rejecting the view that the earlier flight was mentioned by anticipation, since the Church began to move towards the desert well before the empire was divided. Wesley goes furthest, setting out four periods of about eleven hundred, eight hundred and eighty-eight, seven hundred and seventy-seven and six hundred and sixty-six years, and filling the wilderness with a map of conversions: Denmark about 948, Poland and Silesia in 965, all Russia by 980, Hungary in 997, Transylvania about 1000, so that Christianity now reached in an uninterrupted tract from the eastern empire to the western. Barnes locates the persecution rather than the refuge: when Paganism could no longer destroy the church, the same enmity was vented in another form, the rise of the Papacy.
15:
What is the flood? Gill rules out persecution and settles on doctrine: not any before the fall of Paganism, nor the Arian persecution, since this flood is distinguished from that, but the flood of errors and heresies poured in between Constantine and the rise of antichrist — the Arian, which denied the divinity of Christ; the Nestorian, which divided his person; the Eutychian, which confounded his two natures. Clarke takes the water as the book itself later interprets waters, peoples and multitudes and nations, and reads an inundation of barbarous nations: Goths, Heruli, Franks, Huns and Vandals, set against the Christians at the instigation of the pagans remaining there. He borrows a historian’s verdict: the most calamitous period in human history was that between the death of Theodosius the Great and the establishment of the Lombards in Italy, a hundred and seventy-six years.

Barnes will have none of it as natural history. Some serpents are said to eject bile when enraged, and some sea-monsters to spout water, but this is taken from neither: it is the mere product of the imagination, though the sense is clear. Robertson adds that the compound rendered carried away by the river was not coined here but turns up in a papyrus two centuries earlier.

Ellicott notices the change of name: the foe was a dragon for his cruelty, and is now a serpent for his subtlety — the first attack was open persecution, from which she escapes by flight, and the subtlety of the enemy finds another device. His application is the sharpest in the chapter. The woman that cannot be destroyed by open persecution may be swept away by a hostile public opinion; it is not the rulers alone who stand up against the Church, for an infuriated populace may be stirred up, and the temper of the mob occasioned as much suffering in early Christian days as the political authorities. Ill-regulated popular impulses, nominally for Christianity or against it, have done enough of the devil’s work.

On the earth swallowing the river, Clarke and Ellicott reach one law by different roads. Clarke quotes the reversal: nothing was more likely to subvert the Christian Church than the irruption of so many barbarous nations, but the event proved contrary — the barbarians were rather swallowed up by the Romans than the Romans by the barbarians, and the heathen conquerors, instead of imposing their own, submitted to the religion of the conquered, and affected even the laws, the manners and the very name of Romans, so the victors were lost among the vanquished. Ellicott generalises: every devil-born flood of opinion, violence or sentiment sinks beneath the surface; such movements rise like a river, are tasted, and are rejected. It is not one nation or age that is represented but an eternal law, and the finest epic of the world might have for its motto, The earth helped the woman. Barnes keeps it sober: we are not to look for any literal fulfilment, though in the dark ages many such interventions occurred. Robertson mentions the Lycus disappearing underground near Colossae, then adds that the symbol does not depend on such examples.

The last verse turns the war from the body to its members. Barnes states the logic: as he could not destroy the church itself, he vented his malice on all who were its friends — fulfilled in the Inquisition and the deaths of men like Wycliffe and Huss. Ellicott extends it past violence: the foe may cease to assail the collective Church and yet assail Christians by a thousand discomforts, by petty opposition, by undermining their morals, by making them unpopular — not as Christians, but as very particular ones. Robertson keeps to the verb: the dragon went off in his rage, perhaps recalling the enmity promised in Eden, and the two marks named excite the wrath of the devil then and always.
